> 執大象，天下往。往而不害，安平泰.

Chapter 34 said the Dao does not act as master. Chapter 35 moves to the human side: how does a person relate to a Dao like that?

The answer is one character — 執.

And that character has been read wrong for a long time. The usual reading is "grasp": hold a set of principles in your hand and use them to require things of others.

Read that way, the two chapters contradict each other immediately. Chapter 34 said the Dao does not master; chapter 35 would be saying a person should grab the Dao and rule with it.

So the first job is to put 執 back into its original meaning.

## 執 is to take hold of a person

Its original sense is to seize, to arrest — the character contains the hand and the prisoner. 執罪人: to arrest a criminal.

From there it extends: 執中 is to hold to the center oneself; 執一 is to keep to the one. The direction of 執 depends entirely on its object. Arresting someone points outward; holding the center points inward.

執大象 is the second kind. You take hold of it in yourself, not over others.

## 大象 is the whole, not an image

象 in the old usage also means the whole configuration — what is presented as a complete form. 大象 is not a picture of the Dao; it is the Dao as a whole, taken as one thing rather than as a collection of principles.

Which is why 執 works here: you cannot hold a collection; you can only hold a whole.

## 天下往

The world comes. Not "the world obeys" — 往 is to go toward, to visit.

> 往而不害，安平泰.

They come and are not harmed: 安, 平, 泰 — settled, level, at ease.

The absence of harm is doing the actual work. People come to what does not damage them. A position that others approach because approaching is safe is a different kind of authority from one they approach because they must.

## 樂與餌，過客止

Music and bait: the passing traveler stops.

This is the contrast the chapter needs. 樂 and 餌 are the things that hold attention — the pleasure and the offer. They work, and they work only while they are being supplied.

A traveler stopped by bait is stopped, not arrived. Remove the bait and the stop ends.

## 道之出口，淡乎其無味

> 道之出口，淡乎其無味，視之不足見，聽之不足聞，用之不足既.

When the Dao is spoken, it is 淡 — thin, without flavor. Not enough to see, not enough to hear, and inexhaustible in use.

淡 is the property being praised, and it is the least attractive property a thing can have. Bait has flavor. Music has flavor. The Dao, offered, tastes like nothing.

Which is exactly why it does not stop the passing traveler: it gives no reason to stop. And it is why it can be used without end: nothing about it is being consumed.

## The relation between the two

Chapter 34: the Dao does not master, so it can be great.
Chapter 35: a person holds it in himself, so others come without being harmed.

Neither is a technique for attracting people. The attraction is a consequence of not needing them to come.

## A test

Think of the thing you offer that people respond to most reliably. Is it flavor or is it 淡? Both work; only one of them still works when you stop supplying it.
